Comment 4. Regarding CD19-targeting CAR-T cells, since CD19 is a B cell marker,
how to ensure that it is the CD19+ TAM but not the general B cells that got
specifically inhibited by the anti-CD19 CAR-T cells?
Response: We deeply appreciate the reviewer’s critical concern regarding the specificity
of anti-CD19 CAR-T cells for CD19+ TAMs versus normal B cells. This is a pivotal
consideration, as CD19 serves as a canonical B cell marker, and potential off-target
effects on B cells could lead to immunosuppression or other adverse events.
Our preclinical investigations addressed this by using genetically modified μMT mice,
which lack mature B cells due to a mutation in the immunoglobulin μ heavy chain gene. In
these models, administration of anti-CD19 CAR-T cells significantly inhibited
hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression. Flow cytometric analysis confirmed that this
anti-tumor effect was attributed to the selective depletion of CD19⁺ TAMs within the tumor
microenvironment (TME), with no confounding contributions from B cells. (Figure S3F).
These findings provide direct evidence that CD19-targeted CAR-T cells can exert anti-
tumor effects via TAM depletion independent of B cell presence, supporting the feasibility
of TAM-specific targeting.
While μMT mice provide genetic validation of TAM-specific targeting, we acknowledge
the translational challenge of B cell toxicity in clinical settings. To address this, we are
implementing the following complementary strategies:
A. Dual-signal CAR-T design: Engineering CAR-T cells to require a second signal (e.g.,
tumor-specific cytokines or checkpoint molecules) that is only present in the TME.
B. AND-gate CARs: Developing dual-targeting CARs (e.g., CD19 + TAM-specific markers
such as CD163 or MARCO) to reduce off-target B cell depletion.
C. Hypoxia-activated CARs: Exploiting the low-oxygen tumor microenvironment to trigger
CAR-T activity selectively.
D. Intratumoral injection: Directly administering CAR-T cells into tumors (e.g., via
ultrasound or CT-guided intratumoral injection) to enhance local targeting and minimize
systemic exposure.
We are committed to translating these approaches to the clinic and providing a
precision treatment regimen for HCC patients. Thank you again for highlighting this critical
consideration, which has guided our focus on refining CAR-T specificity for clinical
applicability. Please let us know if further details on any of these strategies would
strengthen this aspect of our work.

Comment 6. PAX5 is a pro-B-cell factor and the above-mentioned previous study
(DOI: 10.1038/s41467-022-33117-y) has reported that the deficiency of PAX5 could
drive the macrophage differentiation. The authors should at least discuss how the
current study can be related to that finding. Because here the current study found
a positive role of PAX5 on the PD-L1 expression and tumor immunosuppression in

Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful perspective regarding the relationship
between our identified CD19+ TAMs and previously reported pro-B-cell-derived
macrophages (B-MFs). This comparison provides a valuable framework to contextualize
our findings, and we thank the opportunity to clarify key distinctions and connections:
While prior work has elegantly demonstrated that cancers can induce trans-differentiation
of bone marrow-derived B-cell precursors—specifically Csf1R⁺ Pax5Low pre-B cells and
immature IgM⁺ B cells—into TAMs (termed B-MFs) via M-CSF signaling. A defining
feature of B-MFs is the downregulation of PAX5 alongside upregulation of macrophage-
associated genes (CD68, Csf1r, Cebpb, Cebpg, Ccl2, Csf1), coupled with enhanced
phagocytic and immunosuppressive functions. Notably, these B-MFs are nearly absent
in μMT mice (which lack mature B cells), consistent with their origin from B-cell
lineage precursors.
In our study, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis revealed that CD19+
TAMs exhibit co-expression of B-cell (IGHM, IGHG) and macrophage (CD68, CSF1R)
gene modules (Fig 3C). Furthermore, in vivo studies demonstrate that CD19⁺ TAMs exist
at low frequencies under physiological conditions (see Figure S1D), including in μMT mice
(Figure S3H), and are enriched during tumor progression, where they promote
immunosuppression.
A key mechanistic distinction lies in the role of PAX5. In B-MFs, PAX5 is downregulated
as part of the trans-differentiation process from B-cell precursors to macrophages. In our
study, however, PAX5 functions not as a lineage repressor but as a transcriptional
activator within CD19⁺ TAMs: PAX5 overexpression in macrophages (THP-1 cells)
induces CD19 expression without suppressing macrophage markers (e.g., CD68, CSF1R).
Far from being contradictory, our findings and the prior report on B-MFs collectively
highlight the context-dependent functionality of PAX5 in regulating hematopoietic cell fate
and plasticity. While PAX5 loss drives myeloid commitment in progenitors, its
overexpression in mature macrophages promotes an immunosuppressive, mitochondrial-
rich TAM phenotype. We had expanded the Discussion section (Page 18, Line 11) to
explicitly address this context-dependent functionality and its implications for TAM biology.
Furthermore, our preliminary tracing studies suggest that CD19⁺ macrophages in
tumors originate from two sources: peripheral blood monocytes and tissue-resident
macrophages (For reviewer-Figure 9). However, the relative contribution of each
population remains to be quantified. We will perform more in vivo and in vitro models to
clarify the origination and cell differentiation of CD19+ macrophages in the future.

Reviewer #5：
In this study, the authors compellingly identified CD19⁺ TAMs as a novel,
immunosuppressive subpopulation enriched in HCC and linked to poor prognosis. The
findings are quite innovative and informative, and the paper is well written. There were
several concerns that need to be solved.
Response: We sincerely value your positive assessment of our study. We take your
concerns seriously and are committed to addressing them thoroughly to strengthen the
rigor and impact of our work. Please find below our detailed responses to each concern,
along with the specific revisions we have implemented (or plan to implement) in the revised
manuscript. We hope the revised manuscript will meet your expectations.
Major：
Comment 1. The authors should explicitly compare CD19⁺ TAMs with traditional
M1/M2-like features on their metabolic, transcriptional, and functional identities. Is
there a M2 subpopulation in the single cell mass cytometry (CyTOF) dataset? Are
CD19+ TAMs a subpopulation of M2 macrophages, or phenotypically altered M2
macrophages? Please clarify the relationship between this novel cell population
and traditional macrophage subtypes more directly.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s interest in clarifying the relationship between
CD19⁺/CD19⁻ TAMs and classical M1/M2 polarization states. To address this, we
systematically compared these subsets as detailed.
To compare the classification of CD19⁺/CD19⁻ macrophages with M1/M2 polarization
states, we re-analyzed scRNA-seq data to profile their M1/M2 subtype markers,
inflammatory, metabolic, proliferative, and immune functional signatures. While CD19⁺
macrophages exhibited transcriptional proximity to M2-like macrophages, no strong
correlative associations were observed (Supplementary Table 8; see also Figure 3D).
CyTOF analysis further confirmed the presence of a classical M2-like subpopulation
(CD163⁺) within HCC tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), which is not entirely
identical to CD19⁺ TAMs (For reviewer-Figure 10).
For reviewer-Figure 10. Visualized tSNE representation of the immune cell subtypes in
human HCC tissues, including CD19+ TAMs, CD19- TAMs, and B cells (left) and CD19
protein expression levels in these three clusters. Clusters are differently color-coded and
annotated in the figure. Visualized tSNE representation M2-like subpopulation (CD163+,
right). Data were generated from CyTOF data.
In addition, flow cytometry validation of canonical M1/M2 markers revealed that
CD19⁺ TAMs expressed higher levels of M2-related markers than CD19⁻ TAMs (For
reviewer-Figure 11). However, no definite associations were found between the CD19+/
CD19- TAMs and M1/M2 classifications.
For reviewer-Figure 11. The expression of classical markers of M1 and M2-polarized
macrophages were analyzed for CD19+ TAMs and CD19- TAMs from human HCC
samples. Representative flow cytometry histograms are shown.
These data indicated that the CD19⁺/CD19⁻ axis represents a distinct dimension of
macrophage heterogeneity orthogonal to traditional M1/M2 polarization. Their unique co-
expression of B cell lineage markers, PAX5 dependency, and mitochondrial hyperactivity
further distinguish them as a functionally discrete TAM subset. We are conducting
additional in vivo and in vitro investigations to systematically characterize their
developmental provenance and lineage commitment processes, and clarify the positioning
of CD19⁺ macrophages within the established M1/M2 polarization spectrum.
Comment 2. Could CD19+ macrophages be fused cells between macrophage and B
cells, or macrophage with B cell endocytosed?
Response: We fully acknowledge the critical nature of your concerns and have addressed
the potential fusion or endocytosis hypotheses through a combination of single-cell
imaging, flow cytometry, and genetic modeling. These experiments now provide
conclusive evidence that CD19+ TAMs arise from transcriptional reprogramming rather
than cell fusion.
1) Fluorescence Distribution and Marker Analysis
Single-cell imaging flow cytometry staining and mIHC: High-resolution imaging revealed
non-uniform co-distribution of CD14 (macrophage marker) and CD19 within CD19⁺ TAMs.

endocytosis of intact B cells, which would likely show membrane-bound CD19 signals (Fig
1C). Furthermore, CD19⁺ macrophages were uniformly negative for CD20, another B cell-
specific markers (Fig 1E).
2) Cell Size and Phenotypic Validation
Flow Cytometry Gating: Back-gating analysis of CD19⁺ macrophages exhibit a distinct
FSC/SSC values distribution from B cells (Fig S1C).
3) Genetic Model Validation
In B cell-deficient uMT mouse models, CD19⁺ TAMs were still detected, demonstrating
their development is independent of B cell presence (Fig S3H). This eliminates the
possibility that CD19⁺ expression arises from B cell fusion or phagocytosis, as both
processes would require intact B cells in the microenvironment. In WT mice, CD19⁺ TAMs
frequencies showed no correlation with B cell counts across tumor models (Fig. S1F),
further excluding B cell dependence.
Together, these results indicated that CD19⁺ macrophages were not derived from
macrophage-B cell fusion or B cell endocytosis. Their CD19 expression likely reflects a
unique transcriptional program, as supported by their distinct metabolic, transcriptional,
and functional profiles. Instead, CD19 expression arises from PAX5-driven transcriptional
reprogramming in myeloid cells.
Comment 3. Although the OXPHOS inhibitor IACS-010759 exhibited an improved
anti-tumor effect, the authors could not attribute the function to CD19 macrophages,
since tumor cells or other cells can also be targeted by this inhibitor.
Response： We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's insightful comment concerning the
potential outside-target effects of IACS-010759. As a pharmacological OXPHOS inhibitor,
IACS-010759 may indeed exert effects not only on CD19+ TAMs but also on other cell
types within the tumor microenvironment (TME), including tumor cells and stromal
populations.
However, previous studies have indicated that M2-TAMs exhibit high OXPHOS activity
and are characterized by an enhanced spare respiratory capacity, which supports their
immunosuppressive function (PMID: 33407885, 26649578). In contrast, tumor cells in
hypoxic regions, particularly in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), primarily rely on
glycolysis for energy metabolism (PMID: 29171040, 33398194). More importantly, our
data demonstrate that OXPHOS inhibition combined with anti-PD-L1 treatment
significantly remodels the immune microenvironment (Supplementary figure S12),
specifically by reducing CD19+ TAMs (For reviewer-Figure 12) and enhancing antitumor
immunity. These findings suggest that targeting CD19+ TAMs is a major contributor to the
observed antitumor response.
For reviewer-Figure 12. Representative images showing CD19⁺ TAMs abundance in
HCC tissue sections from control mice (n=5) and mice treated with OXPHOS inhibition
combined with anti-PD-L1 (n=5). CD19⁺ TAMs are identified as CD19⁺CD68⁺ double-
positive cells (white arrows). Scale bar = 50 μm. (Right) Quantitative analysis of CD19⁺
TAMs abundance in the two groups. Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Statistical
analysis was performed using unpaired two-tailed t-test, **P < 0.01.
While we cannot definitively ascribe the entire therapeutic effect exclusively to CD19+
TAMs, we revised the wording as “Collectively, therapeutic approaches targeting
CD73 or OXPHOS -when optimized to leverage the heightened dependency of
CD19+ TAMs on these pathways show great promise for improving the anti-tumor
efficacy of immunotherapy for HCC.” in the manuscript to ensure more precise
descriptions of this relationship. Additionally, we plan to conduct further experiments to
dissect the cell type-specific effects of IACS-010759 in future studies, which will help
clarify the contributions of different cell populations to the therapeutic outcome.
Comment 4. The last sentence “Collectively, therapeutic approaches targeting
CD73 or OXPHOS in CD19 + TAMs show great promise for improving the anti-tumor
efficacy of immunotherapy for HCC.” is not acceptable. The authors need to discuss
more about how their findings could translate to therapeutical approaches.
OXPHOS and CD73 are all non-specific to CD19 macrophages and might not be
good targets for developing new therapies.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s critical and insightful comments, which
highlight a key consideration for translating our findings into therapeutic strategies. We
fully agree that OXPHOS and CD73 are not exclusive to CD19⁺ TAMs, and their non-
specificity poses challenges for the development of targeted therapies.
While OXPHOS and CD73 are not unique to CD19⁺ TAMs, our data reveal that CD19⁺
TAMs in HCC exhibit a selectively heightened dependency on these pathways to exert
their immunosuppressive functions. Specifically, CD19⁺ TAMs display significantly higher
OXPHOS activity and CD73 expression compared to CD19⁻ TAMs, whereas HCC tumor
cells primarily rely on glycolysis—consistent with their hypoxic microenvironment. Notably,
CD19⁺ TAMs and HCC cells show comparable levels of CD73 and PD-L1 expression (For
reviewer-Figure 13), our functional data highlight a distinct role of CD19⁺ TAMs in
mediating the effects of these pathways: in vivo studies using Pax5△MΦ mice (which
specifically deplete CD19⁺ TAMs) demonstrated that blockade of PD-L1 and CD73 no
longer impacted tumor progression (Figure S10F). This suggests that CD19⁺ TAMs are
critical mediators of the immunosuppressive effects exerted by these molecules.
For-reviewer-Figure 13. The expression of CD73 and PD-L1 on CD19+ TAMs and HCC
cells.
Moreover, reports indicate that mitochondrial drugs containing triphenylphosphine
(TPP⁺) exert effects not only on tumor cells but also on other immunosuppressive cells
within the tumor microenvironment (TME), such as myeloid-derived suppressor cells
(MDSCs) and regulatory T cells (Tregs) (PMID: 34189437, 37172686). Therefore, we
propose that small-molecule inhibitors typically act on multiple cell types in vivo; however,
the intensity of their biological effects varies significantly depending on the expression
abundance of the target in different cells and the degree of cellular dependence on the
target’s function.
We acknowledge that our original conclusion overstated the direct therapeutic potential
of these targets without sufficiently addressing their broad expression profiles. We will
revise it to: “Collectively, therapeutic approaches targeting CD73 or OXPHOS -when
optimized to leverage the heightened dependency of CD19⁺ TAMs on these
pathways show great promise for improving the anti-tumor efficacy of
immunotherapy for HCC.” In addition, our results from the preclinical HCC model
indicate significant translational potential for CD19-targeted CAR-T therapy in treating
solid tumors with high levels of CD19+ TAMs independent of B cell presence. We are
currently launching an investigator-initiated trial (IIT) to test the efficacy of anti-CD19 CAR-
T cells for HCC treatment.
Thank you again for highlighting this critical point, which will significantly strengthen
the translational rigor of our manuscript.
Minor:
1. In figure 4A, p-value needs to be provided.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s attention to statistical clarity. For this figure
(CD19⁺ Mφ/CD19⁻ Mφ mitochondrial gene expression ratios), the y - axis represents the
fold-change in expression of CD19⁺ macrophages relative to CD19⁻ macrophages for
each mitochondrial gene. As observed, most mitochondrial genes display a trend of
relatively higher expression in CD19⁺ TAMs, consistent with our initial observation.
We acknowledge that only a limited number of these genes reach statistical
significance. However, the consistent trend of upregulated mitochondrial gene expression
in CD19⁺ TAMs still served as a critical preliminary observation. This collective pattern
provided a strong rationale to pursue subsequent functional studies exploring whether
CD19⁺ TAMs possess distinct mitochondrial properties, which we further investigated and
validated in downstream experiments.
Thank you for highlighting this important consideration, which has helped us present
the data more transparently.
Comment 2. In figure 7A, the authors should clarify the differences between the
upper and bottom panel.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to clarify the figure. In Figure 7A:
The upper panel shows in situ images of tumors within the liver (i.e., tumors remain
attached to the liver parenchyma without dissection). The lower panel displays images of
the same tumors after complete dissection and isolation from the liver tissue. This
distinction helps visualize both the natural tumor location within the organ and the intact
tumor morphology post-dissection. We have revised the figure legend to explicitly state
this difference:
Revised Figure 7A Legend:
Hepa1-6 cells (5× 105) were mixed with iBMDMs (with or without Pax5 overexpression) at
a ratio of 1:1, and orthotopically injected into the livers of C57BL/6 mice. Tumor images
and sizes were showed at 15 days post-inoculation. Tumor sites were indicated by red
dotted line in liver. Upper panel: Tumors in situ (attached to liver tissue). Lower panel: The
same tumors after complete dissection from the liver. n = 5 per group.
Thank you for prompting this clarification to improve figure interpretability.
3. Gr1+ cells need to be introduced and the biological significance should be
explained.
Response： We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to clarify the role of Gr1⁺ cells in
our model. Gr1⁺ cells are a heterogeneous population of immunosuppressive myeloid
cells that typically inhibit T cell activation and promote tumor immune evasion. Clinically,
high infiltration of Gr1⁺ cells correlated with poor responses to immunotherapies such as
anti-PD-1 antibodies, making them critical regulators of the tumor microenvironment.
In orthotopic syngeneic mouse models, Gr-1+ cells were more abundant in tumors with the
presence of CD19+ TAMs (Figures S3C). In our comparative analysis of Pax5flox/flox-Lyz-
cre mice and wild-type (WT) controls mice, we also observed that a higher abundance of
CD19⁺ TAMs was concomitant increased infiltration of Gr1⁺ cells in TME (For reviewer-
Figure 14). These findings suggests that CD19⁺ TAMs may recruit Gr1⁺
immunosuppressive cells to foster a pro-tumorigenic TME.
For reviewer-Figure 14. Correlation analysis between CD19+ TAMs and Gr-1+ cells in
mice HCC tissues. n = 14. Pearson correlation test was used.
We acknowledge that our initial focus on CD19⁺ TAMs and T cell interactions led us
to underemphasize Gr1⁺ cells. and this will be a focus of our Discussion section (Page
19, line 17) and follow-up studies. Please do not hesitate to contact us if you have any
further questions or require additional clarification. We are happy to provide more details
to address any concerns.
Thank you again for all reviewers’ guidance and support for our manuscript. We believe
these revisions have substantially improved the manuscript’s scientific validity, clarity, and
suitability for publication in Nature Communications. We look forward to your favorable
evaluation of the revised manuscript and happy to provide further clarification,
additional
data, or minor adjustments promptly as needed.
Sincerely,

Dear Editor and Reviewers,
We sincerely appreciate the editorial board for providing us with the valuable
opportunity to revise our manuscript. We also wish to express our heartfelt
gratitude to all reviewers for their careful and rigorous evaluation of our work
amid their busy schedules, as well as for their constructive comments and
suggestions. We have carefully studied and fully addressed each comment.
Detailed point-by-point responses to the reviewers’ comments are provided
below.
Reviewer #1 - Remarks to Author
The authors, supporting the clinical applicability of the biomarker, present a
low-quality image that makes it difficult to determine which cells are truly
immunoreactive, and even more so to distinguish between macrophages and other
stromal cells. Furthermore, despite being requested, they do not provide a cutoff point
for considering the marker positive in clinical practice. The suggested diagnostic
approach seems more suitable for analysis with flow cytometry rather than on human
tissues.
Response: Thank you again for your critical and constructive comments, which have
guided us to clarify key details of our research. We have carefully addressed your
concerns regarding image quality and the cutoff value for CD19⁺ macrophage
identification, incorporating specific experimental contexts and supplementary
materials as follows:
1) We fully acknowledge your observation that the image quality in the submission
hindered the identification of immunoreactive cells and cell type distinction. To meet
the file size limit for manuscript attachments, we had to compress the original images,
which inadvertently compromised the clarity of cellular morphological details.We have
supplied original high-resolution Figures as attachments (in PDF format). These
uncompressed images and annotated figures ensure that the morphology of CD19⁺
macrophages and their distinction from other cells are readily observable, especially
in Figure 1.
2) Regarding your request for a cutoff value for CD19 positivity in clinical practice, we
would like to clarify that a universal fixed cutoff is not feasible due to inherent
variability in experimental systems, e.g., batch differences in antibody affinity,
variations in tissue fixation time across clinical samples, or subtle adjustments to
staining protocols. We have established a contextual, clinically validated identification
standard based on relative expression and cell type co-localization of CD68 and
CD19. The specific criteria are as follows: CD19⁺macrophage or CD19 expression
in macrophages (pre-identified by CD68 positivity, large irregular cytoplasm,
and eccentric nuclei) is defined by comparing it to the "gold standard" of CD19
expression in B cells. This standard is directly applied in our ongoing phase I/II
CD19 CAR-T trial for advanced liver cancer (NCT03732547). Prior to CD19 CAR-T
infusion, we perform multi-color IHC (CD68/CD19/DAPI) on patients’ tumor tissue
samples to quantify CD19⁺ macrophages. Tissues are sectioned and stained,
CD19⁺ macrophages are strictly counted as CD68⁺ cells meeting the above CD19
expression (relative to B cells).
Aligns with routine clinical pathology workflows: FFPE sections are standard for
tumor diagnosis, and our multi-color IHC protocol can be implemented in most clinical
laboratories with basic immunostaining equipment.
We deeply appreciate your patience and guidance in helping us refine these
critical details. The supplementary original images and clarified identification criteria
will significantly enhance the reproducibility and clinical relevance of our work. We
hope they fully addresses your concerns and look forward to your further feedback.

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed
reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in
peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who
co-review manuscripts.

reviewers, which has helped strengthen our manuscript. We have carefully addressed
all comments and revised the manuscript accordingly, with detailed responses
included in the rebuttal letter. Please let us know if any further information or
clarification is required.
Reviewer #3 - Remarks to the Author
The authors have sufficiently addressed all my comments except one minor point. In
their point-by-point response pdf (p.13) addressing our comment 2, for their "For
reviewer Figure 4" panel B's WB for PDL1, it looks like that upon the pulldown of
HSC70, it failed to show altered binding for the PD-L1 mutants. I am not sure if they
have pasted a wrong WB by mistake, as the leftmost lane for "IP" also has band for
PD-L1 but the "IB" one does not.

pattern in the WB for PD-L1 in "For reviewer Figure 4" panel B. During Co-IP
experiments, we initially attempted to pulldown HSC70 using PD-L1 as the bait but
were unable to obtain interpretable WB results, likely due to the presence of multiple
modified forms of PD-L1 leading to complex co-precipitated protein mixtures. We
therefore switched to pulldown of PD-L1 using HSC70 as the bait (as presented in the

to HSC70, which aligns with our conclusion. We apologize for any confusion caused
by the initial experimental design. Please let us know if further clarification is needed.

1. According to the scRNA-seq data presented in Reviewer Figure 10, CD19⁺
macrophages exhibited substantial overlap with traditional M2 macrophages,
although they were not entirely identical. This observation may diminish the novelty of
the study, given that these CD19⁺ macrophages were also found to be functionally
similar to M2 macrophages in mediating immunosuppression. Consequently, the key
findings of this study—the upregulation of Pax5 and CD19 in this macrophage
subpopulation—may represent merely new markers for an M2-like subtype. However,
these markers lack sufficient specificity, as they demonstrate poor selectivity in
distinguishing these cells from B cells.
Response: We greatly appreciate your insightful comment on the scRNA-seq data
and the novelty of our study. Your observation regarding the overlap between CD19⁺
macrophages and traditional M2 macrophages, as well as the specificity of
Pax5/CD19 markers, has prompted us to conduct a more in-depth analysis and
clarification, which we present in detail below:
1) We fully agree with your finding that CD19⁺macrophages show substantial overlap
with traditional M2 macrophages. However, we emphasize that CD19⁺
macrophages are not merely a "subset of M2 macrophages" but a distinct
subpopulation with unique molecular and functional features that distinguish
them from canonical M2 macrophages, which is a key basis for the novelty of our
study.
Numerous single-cell analyses of human and mouse samples have revealed that
the status of macrophages is not a simple M1/M2 dichotomy as in vitro, but a
continuous spectrum. In some cases, M1 and M2 phenotypes of macrophages may
express “opposing” markers at the same time in vivo. CD19+ macrophages were
observed to co-express established M1 and M2 markers and the scRNA-seq data
highlighted the involvement of both CD19+ macrophage-specific and B cell-related
transcription factors in their differentiation. We belive that CD19⁺macrophages are
a functionally distinct subpopulation, not just a "M2-like subtype", their unique
transcriptional and functional traits provide new insights into the heterogeneity
of immunosuppressive macrophages in the tumor microenvironment.
2) We acknowledge your concern that Pax5 and CD19 alone lack sufficient
specificity to distinguish CD19⁺macrophages from B cells (given that both markers
are canonical B cell lineage markers). However, in our study, when PAX5 was
overexpressed in B cells, we observed that it failed to upregulate the expression
levels of CD73 and PD-L1. While the function of CD19 expression in
macrophages remains unclear to us at present, the upregulation of Pax5 and
CD19 in macrophages is not merely a "new marker for M2-like cells", it
represents a novel lineage reprogramming event in macrophages that has not
been reported previously in HCC. We are currently engaged in active exploration of
the associated differentiation between PAX5/CD19 expression and macrophages.
For reviewer Figure #2-1. B cells were overexpressed with Pax5, the relative protein
expression of PAX5, CD19, CD73 and PD-L1 were showed.
In summary, while CD19⁺macrophages share some immunosuppressive
features with M2 macrophages, their unique transcriptional program, functional
mechanisms, and Pax5/CD19-driven lineage reprogramming distinguish them as a
novel subpopulation. The multi-marker identification panel we established fully
addresses the specificity concern for Pax5/CD19 markers. We believe these
clarifications further highlight the novelty and clinical relevance of our study.Thank you
again for your valuable feedback, which has helped us strengthen the rigor and clarity
of our work. We look forward to your further comments.
2. Furthermore, the translational significance of this study remains unclear. The
authors propose targeting OXPHOS and CD73; however, these targets are not
exclusive to CD19⁺ TAMs. Although the authors attempted to eliminate CD19⁺
macrophages using CD19 CAR-T cells in mature B cell-depleted mice, this approach
itself is not ideal for translation, as CD19 CAR-T therapy carries significant risks and is
not targeted.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comments on the translational significance of
our study. We fully understand your concerns about the specificity of OXPHOS/CD73
targets and the translational feasibility of CD19 CAR-T therapy, and we would like to
clarify and supplement the relevant details based on our research data and ongoing
clinical practice:
1) We acknowledge that OXPHOS and CD73 are not exclusive to CD19⁺
macrophages, but our study confirms that macrophages (especially CD19⁺
macrophages) are the main contributors to OXPHOS activity and CD73 expression in
the tumor microenvironment (TME) of liver cancer, which provides a practical basis for
the translational potential of targeting these molecules.
As shown in For-reviewer-Figure 12 and 13, although OXPHOS and CD73 are
not exclusive to CD19⁺macrophages, targeting them will primarily affect CD19⁺
macrophages (the main functional contributors in TME) . This "functional specificity"
is sufficient to support their translational value, especially in combination with
immunotherapy to further enhance targeting accuracy.
2) We acknowledge that traditional CD19 CAR-T cell therapy carries risks, such as
off-target effects on B cells. However, our research and ongoing clinical trials focus on
optimizing the application of CD19 CAR-T cell therapy in solid tumors (particularly
HCC) by regulating infusion doses; in the future, dual-CAR strategies may also be
explored. This approach aims to minimize B cell-associated toxicity while ensuring
therapeutic efficacy against CD19⁺macrophages, proposing a key practical
exploration to advance its clinical translation.
In conclusion, based on the dominant role of CD19⁺macrophages in TME's
OXPHOS activity and CD73 function, targeting these molecules can primarily
affect CD19⁺macrophages, providing a feasible strategy for reversing TME
immunosuppression. Through preclinical dose optimization and ongoing
clinical trials, CD19 CAR-T can safely and effectively target CD19⁺
macrophages in HCC, providing a new personalized treatment option for
patients with high CD19⁺ macrophages levels.
We believe that these explorations address the key issues of translational
feasibility and provide a solid foundation for the clinical application of our findings.
Thank you again for your valuable comments, which have helped us further improve
the rigor and clinical relevance of our research. We look forward to your further
feedback.

## Paper

## Abstract

Tumor-associated macrophages are a key component that contributes to the immunosuppressive microenvironment in human cancers. However, therapeutic targeting of macrophages has been a challenge in clinic due to the limited understanding of their heterogeneous subpopulations and distinct functions. Here, we identify a clinically relevant CD19+ subpopulation of macrophages that is enriched in many types of cancer, particularly in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The CD19+ macrophages exhibit increased levels of programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) and CD73, enhanced mitochondrial oxidation, and compromised phagocytosis, indicating their immunosuppressive functions. Targeting CD19+ macrophages with anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T (SCAR-T) cells inhibited HCC tumor growth. We identify Paired Box 5 (PAX5) as a primary driver of up-regulated mitochondrial biogenesis in CD19+ macrophages, which depletes cytoplasmic Ca2+, leading to lysosomal deficiency and consequent accumulation of CD73 and PD-L1. Inhibiting CD73 or mitochondrial oxidation enhanced the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade therapy in treating HCC, suggesting great promise for CD19+ macrophage-targeting therapeutics.

---

## Introduction

Liver cancer has emerged as the third leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide, with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) being the predominant pathological subtype1. Current therapies for treating HCC comprise surgical resection, liver transplantation, locoregional therapies, and systemic treatments including targeted therapies and immunotherapy2. Surgical resection and liver transplantation offer the best chance for a cure, but are only options for a small subset of patients diagnosed at an early stage. Locoregional therapies, including radiofrequency ablation and transarterial chemoembolization, are used for intermediate stages of HCC or when surgery is not feasible. Systemic treatments, like tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g., sorafenib and lenvatinib) and immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., atezolizumab, nivolumab and pembrolizumab), have expanded treatment options for the majority of patients with advanced HCC that misses the window for surgical intervention3. Despite these advancements, the 5-year overall survival rates for HCC remain below 20%4. These therapies face significant challenges in the clinic, including tumor heterogeneity, which leads to variable treatment responses, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), which hampers the efficacy of immunotherapies5,6.

The immunosuppressive microenvironment of HCC is characterized by a complex interplay of various cell types that collectively inhibit effective anti-tumor immune responses. Key players include myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), which accumulate and inhibit T cell activation7. Regulatory T cells (Tregs) suppress cytotoxic T cell function, while cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) produce extracellular matrix components and cytokines that further support an immunosuppressive milieu8. Particularly, tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are the most abundant in HCC that promotes tumor growth and suppresses inflammation9. These various types of stroma cells interact through direct contact and the release of soluble factors, creating a TME that hinders immune-mediated tumor eradication10.

Macrophages exhibit different features in the presence of different inducers, such as lipopolysaccharide and interleukin-4, which lead to the two classic polarizations of macrophages, defining as M1 and M2 macrophages11. TAMs are believed to promote tumor progression by reprogramming local immunosuppression, inducing angiogenesis and drug resistance, and promoting tumor cell invasion. Phenotypically, despite being considered to have an M2-like polarization12, TAMs are noncanonical and dynamically altered in response to stimuli within the TME. Consequently, the binary classification of macrophages is inadequate for describing them within the highly heterogeneous TME, both spatially and temporally13. Studies have identified specific TAM subgroups, such as PD-1+ TAMs in colon cancer, TREM1+ TAMs in hepatocellular carcinoma, and CD169+ TAMs in glioblastoma14-16. These subgroups have diverse or even contradictory effects on tumor progression, suggesting that precise interventions targeting certain TAM subgroups, rather than the wholesale removal of M1, M2 or all TAMs in the TME, are likely to achieve better anti-tumor efficacy. Therefore, understanding the full spectrum of TAMs is crucial for developing therapeutic approaches that target macrophages in HCC.

In the present study, we identified a subgroup of CD19+ TAMs that are enriched in a number of solid tumor types, particularly in HCC. As a transmembrane glycoprotein, CD19 is considered as a biomarker and functionally crucial for the regulation of B cell receptor signaling in both the early and late stages of B cell development. Interestingly, a recent analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data defined a transdifferentiated cell types in the ischemic brain that was characterized by co-expression of B-cell markers and several macrophage markers17, suggesting a potential role of CD19 in macrophages. Here, we elucidated the clinical relevance, cellular functions, and molecular features of CD19+ TAMs and determined the underlying regulatory mechanisms of their immunosuppressive characteristics. Based on these findings, we propose that targeting CD19+ TAMs or mitigating their pro-tumoral effects could be a promising strategy for treating HCC.

## Results

CD19+ macrophages are enriched in HCC
A group of tumor tissue samples (n = 30) from patients with HCC were analyzed with mass cytometry (CyTOF) for profiling their tumor immune microenvironment 6. Unexpectedly, we identified a subgroup of TAMs expressing CD19 at a level comparable to that in B cells in the tumors (Fig. 1A). To validate the presence of CD19+ TAMs, we further conducted immune profiling analysis of HCC samples in a 41-patient cohort. Approximately a half (29 out of 41) of the HCC samples had a considerable proportion (>20% of total TAMs) of CD19+ TAMs. The existence of a CD19+ subpopulation in the TAMs was further confirmed using immunofluorescence (Fig. 1B), ImageStream (Fig. 1C and Supplementary Fig.1A) and flow cytometry (Fig. 1D and Supplementary Fig.1B). Additionally, we applied multiplex immunohistochemical (mIHC) staining on tumors and their adjacent normal tissues using CD14, CD68, CD19, and CD20 markers to demonstrate CD19+ TAMs at the single-cell level (Fig. 1E). Conventional macrophage markers, CD11b and CD68/CD14, were used to confirm their macrophage identity. Notably, the proportion of CD19+ TAMs was much higher in HCC than in adjacent normal tissue or peripheral blood (Fig. 1B and 1D). In terms of cell size, the CD19+ TAMs had greater FSC/SSC (forward scatter/side scatter) values in flow cytometry than those of B cells, suggesting their macrophage cell lineage rather than a B cell lineage (Supplementary Fig.1C).

Next, we wanted to determine whether CD19+ TAMs exist in other types of solid tumors. In a total of six types of human solid tumors, including HCC, CD19+ TAMs are enriched (Fig. 1F) compared with those in peripheral blood and normal tissues. In particular, HCC, renal carcinoma, colorectal cancer, pancreatic cancer, and gastric cancer had a median proportion of CD19+ TAMs over 20% of total TAMs. Similarly, we detected CD19+ macrophages in various normal tissues and peripheral blood in mice (Supplementary Fig.1D). Moreover, the proportion of CD19+ macrophages did not correlate with that of B cells in these tissues (Supplementary Fig. 1E and 1F), further suggesting that they are not derived from B cells. The results collectively suggest that CD19+ macrophages naturally exist in the body but are enriched in solid tumors.

CD19+ TAMs are associated with poor clinical outcomes in HCC
As no previous study reported this subgroup of TAMs, we wanted to examine the clinical relevance of CD19+ macrophages in HCC. A human HCC tissue microarray was co-immunostained with anti-CD19 and anti-CD68 antibodies (Supplementary Fig. 2A). In a total of 191 tissue samples with valid co-immunostaining, we found that the abundance (shown as density) of CD19+ TAMs was positively correlated with tumor size (Supplementary Fig. 2B) and tumor cell differentiation (Supplementary Fig. 2C), but not with disease stages (Supplementary Fig. 2D), suggesting CD19+ TAMs may be recruited at early stage of tumor initiation for creating immunosuppressive TME. Importantly, HCC patients with greater density of CD19+ TAMs had worse overall survival (hazard ratio 3.12, 95% confidential interval 1.23–7.89) and disease-free survival (Fig. 2A and Supplementary Fig. 2E). By contrast, the density of total TAMs had no correlation with overall survival of these patients (Fig. 2B). Consistent with its clinical relevance, the density of CD19+ TAMs was positively correlated with tumor cell proliferation, as indicated by Ki-67 staining in human HCC samples (Fig. 2C). TME analysis of the HCC tissue microarray indicated that a high density of CD19+ TAMs was associated with increased infiltration of Tregs but reduced infiltration of CD8+ T cells (Supplementary Fig. 2F). Collectively, these results demonstrated that CD19+ TAMs correlate with poor clinical prognosis in patients with HCC, underlying a potential modification of TME.

CD19+ TAMs possess immunosuppressive abilities and promote HCC growth
To study the role of CD19+ TAMs in shaping the TME, we further analyzed the CyTOF data from the 41 patients with HCC (the same cohort analyzed in Fig. 1A). CD19+ TAMs represent a major subgroup of TAMs, accounting for approximately 30% of TAMs and 5% of CD45+ cells in the tumors (Supplementary Fig. 2G). The CD19+ and CD19- subsets of TAMs showed a sharp difference at the level of the M2 macrophage marker CD163 (Supplementary Fig. 2H). The proportion of CD19+ TAMs was also negatively correlated with the abundance of total T, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Supplementary Fig. 2I). In-depth analysis showed that the proportion of CD19+ TAMs was positively correlated with that of PD-1+ effector memory T cells (TEMs), but negatively correlated with that of CD127+ TEMs (Supplementary Fig. 2I). These data strongly suggest that CD19+ TAMs possess immunosuppressive abilities.

To determine the role of CD19+ macrophages in tumor growth in vivo, we isolated CD19+ and CD19- macrophages from mouse spleen and mixed them with mouse HCC cells (Hepa 1-6) to generate orthotopic syngeneic mouse models (Supplementary Fig. 3A). The presence of CD19+ macrophages significantly promoted tumor growth in comparison to CD19- macrophages (Fig. 2D). Meanwhile, the number of infiltrating CD8+ T cells was much lower, but Gr-1+ cells were more abundant in tumors with CD19+ macrophages (Supplementary Fig. 3B and 3C). To test the clinical potential of targeting CD19+ macrophages in HCC, we developed mouse chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cells specifically targeting mouse CD19 (see details in Supplementary Methods) for adoptive T cell therapy (Supplementary Fig. 3D). The growth of the tumors with CD19+ macrophages, but not with CD19- macrophages, was significantly inhibited when the tumor-bearing mice received anti-CD19 CAR-T cells. This inhibition was not observed in the mice treated with control CAR-T cells for tumors containing either CD19+ or CD19- macrophages (Fig. 2E and Supplementary Fig. 3E). To exclude the possibility that the inhibition is associated with B cells that are also positive for CD19, we tested the anti-tumor effect of the anti-CD19 CAR-T in muMT mice that lack mature B cells18. Low levels of B cells in muMT mice were verified by flow cytometry (Supplementary Fig. 3F). GFP+ anti-CD19 CAR-T cells were infiltrated into tumors in muMT mice (Supplementary Fig. 3G) and CD19+ macrophages were effectively depleted by the anti-CD19 CAR-T treatment (Supplementary Fig. 3H) The similar anti-tumor effect of anti-CD19 CAR-T cells was observed in the tumors with CD19+ macrophages (Fig. 2F), independent of the B cell levels in the mice. These results highlight the role of CD19+ macrophages in HCC progression and suggested CD19+ macrophages are a potential clinical target for HCC treatment.

CD19+ TAMs exhibit a distinct gene expression profile
To understand the molecular features of CD19+ macrophages, we isolated CD19+ TAMs, CD19- TAMs and B cells from three HCC patients, and conducted scRNA-seq analysis for a total of 52,749 cells (Fig. 3AC and Supplementary Fig. 4A). TAMs were annotated by a high expression level of CD11b, CD14 and CD68, while B cells were identified by CD45, CD19 and CD79A. CD19+ TAMs, CD19- TAMs and B cells were clustered (Fig. 3B). We next characterized the transcriptional profiles of the three types of cells (Fig. 3C). CD19+ TAMs exhibited a distinctive gene signature, among which ribonuclease 1 (RNASE1), selenoprotein P (SELENOP) and apolipoprotein E (APOE) are closely associated with cell metabolism. CD19- TAMs expressed high levels of genes encoding small calcium-binding proteins in the S100 family including S100A9, S100A8 and S100A4. Interestingly, CD19+ TAMs and B cells both express high levels of genes (IGHG1, IGLC1 and IGKC) encoding immunoglobin proteins. Furthermore, CD19+ TAMs appeared to be in proximity to M2-like macrophages, while CD19- TAMs were close to M1 macrophages to some extent, although no definite associations were found (Fig. 3D and Supplementary Fig. 4B). Genes in metabolic pathways and lysosome were significantly enriched in CD19+ TAMs (Fig. 3E). Specifically, CD19+ TAMs had higher expression levels of genes associated with mitochondrial functions and higher mitochondria scores (Fig. 3F and 3G). The gene expression profiling analysis demonstrated that CD19+ macrophages are a subgroup of cells distinct from CD19- macrophages and B cells.

Based on the scRNA-seq data analysis, we identified a 10-gene signature capable of distinguishing between CD19+ and CD19- macrophages. This signature includes five genes specific to CD19+ TAMs (RNASE1, APOE, APOA2, APOC1, SELENOP) and five genes specific to CD19- TAMs (S100A9, S100A8, S100A4, FCN1, VCAN) (Supplementary Fig. 4C). The mRNA expression profiles of these 10 genes effectively differentiate CD19+ TAMs from CD19- TAMs, aligning well with their protein levels determined by flow cytometry (Supplementary Fig. 4D and 4E). This 10-gene signature was also applied to analyze two public scRNA-seq datasets (Bioproject: PRJCA010606 and PRJCA007744) (Supplementary Fig. 5A-5C and 6A-6C). The defined CD19+ TAMs are highly enriched in HCC compared to normal adjacent tissues and show a higher level of mitochondrial activity than CD19- TAMs (Supplementary Fig. 5D, 5E and 6D, 6E).

CD19+ TAMs are highly proliferative and immunosuppressive
Given the high mitochondria score of CD19+ TAMs in HCC, we next analyzed the metabolic activity of mitochondria based on the expression levels of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)-related genes, including NADH dehydrogenase members, cytochrome c oxidase subunit members, and ATP synthase membrane subunit members in CD19+ TAMs and CD19- TAMs. Overall, a majority of these genes was significantly up-regulated in CD19+ TAMs (Fig. 4A). To further characterize the metabolic phenotype of CD19⁺ TAMs, we sorted CD19⁺ and CD19⁻ TAMs from human HCC tissues and subjected to mitochondrial mass staining and reactive oxygen species (ROS) staining. Results revealed that CD19+ TAMs exhibit enhanced mitochondrial mass, accompanied by increased ROS production relative to CD19⁻ TAMs (Supplementary Fig. 7A and 7B). Moreover, we found that CD19+ TAMs exhibit increased co-expression of COX-IV, a key subunit of mitochondrial complex IV, supporting the maintenance of robust OXPHOS activity in CD19+ TAMs (Supplementary Fig. 7C). Seahorse analysis of cell metabolism showed remarkably enhanced mitochondrial respiration of CD19+ macrophages, including both basal and maximal respiratory capacities (Fig. 4B). The energetic feature of CD19+ macrophages may lead to the alterations of their functions and cell activities. First, CD19+ TAMs showed much compromised phagocytotic activity (Fig.S 4C). Second, we found that the proportion of CD19+ TAMs was significantly higher in large tumors than in small ones in an HCC syngeneic mouse model (Supplementary Fig. 7D), consistent with their clinical relevance in human HCC. CD19+ TAMs showed higher levels of Ki-67 expression than CD19- TAMs from the same tumor, both in mice and patients (Supplementary Fig. 7E and 7F). The enhanced proliferation of CD19+ TAMs was confirmed using an orthotopic mouse model and 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU) assays (Supplementary Fig. 7G). Therefore, we reasoned that abundance of CD19+ TAMs in tumors, especially large ones, is likely due to their high proliferation rate.

As CD19+ TAMs are a biomarker for poor clinical outcomes of HCC, we found increased PD-L1 levels in CD19+ TAMs compared to CD19- TAMs (Fig. 4D). During the HCC metabolite analysis6, we were particularly interested in adenosine, a primary immunosuppressive metabolite presents in high levels in the TME of most solid tumors19. In the metabolite data from the analysis using liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), we observed significant associations between the concentrations of adenosine diphosphate (ADP), adenosine monophosphate (AMP), and adenosine and the abundance of CD19+ TAMs in human HCC tumors (Supplementary Fig. 7H). Factors that contribute to adenosine production include hypoxia, high cell turnover, and particularly, the expression of CD73, a 5′-nucleotidase (NT5E) that converts autocrine and paracrine danger signals of ATP to anti-inflammatory adenosine20. Given its pivotal role in regulating the ADP/AMP/adenosine conversion21, CD73 has been an emerging therapeutic target for immune checkpoint blockade22, 23, and numerous CD73-targeted antibodies and small-molecule inhibitors are currently undergoing clinical testing for cancer therapy24. As expected, we observed significantly elevated levels of CD73 in CD19+ TAMs (Fig. 4D). Biochemical assay verified a high 5′-nucleotidase activity of CD73 in the CD19+ TAMs (Fig. 4E). As an indicator of their immunosuppressive functions, CD19+ macrophages significantly inhibited the proliferation of total T cells, CD4+ T cells, and CD8+ T cells when these cells were isolated from the clinical tumor samples and co-cultured in vitro in mixed lymphocyte reaction (MLR) assays (Fig. 4F).

PAX5 is a master regulator for CD19+ macrophages
CD19 is important for B cell development and differentiation25. Therefore, it is intriguing to determine whether CD19 expression is essential for the immunosuppressive activity of CD19+ TAMs. To this end, CD19△Mφ (CD19flox/flox;Lyz-Cre) mice were generated to establish orthotopic mouse HCC tumor models with macrophage-specific knockout of CD19. Unexpectedly, no differences in orthotopic tumor growth were observed between CD19△Mφ mice and their littermate controls (Fig. 5A), although CD19 expression was depleted in literally all the macrophages in the CD19△Mφ mice (Fig. 5B). These results suggest that CD19 can only be used as a biomarker for the CD19+ macrophages, but functionally dispensable for this subgroup of macrophages in the tumor. Among upstream regulators of CD19, PAX5 is the key transcription factor that governs the expression of CD1926, 27. We found that CD19+ TAMs indeed had up-regulated expression of PAX5 at both mRNA and protein levels (Fig. 5C-5E). Thus, we reasoned that PAX5 may play a role in the CD19+ macrophages. Exogenous overexpression of PAX5 in human THP-1 cells (a model for macrophage-related cell activities) induced the expression of CD19, CD73 and PD-L1 (Fig. 5F and 5G). Similar results were observed in mouse immortalized bone marrow-derived macrophages (iBMDMs) (Fig. 5H). Functionally, overexpression of PAX5 impaired phagocytosis in the mouse iBMDMs (Supplementary Fig. 8A). Collectively, PAX5 appears to be a master regulator for the essential features of CD19+ macrophages in the tumor.

In the human THP-1 cells, overexpression of PAX5 also profoundly enhanced mitochondrial respiration in terms of basal respiration, maximal respiration and ATP production (Fig. 5I). Electron microscopy analysis demonstrated that the number of mitochondria was much higher in the THP-1 cells with PAX5 overexpression (Fig. 5J). The increased number of mitochondria and decreased mitochondrial superoxide levels were detected by flow cytometry in these cells ( Fig. 5K). Importantly, PAX5 significantly enhanced the expression of PGC-1α, a potent inducer of mitochondrial biogenesis (Supplementary Fig. 8B)28. Additionally, PAX5-overexpressing THP-1 cells presented a higher level of adenosine in the culture medium than control cells, consistent with increased CD73 activity (Supplementary Fig. 8C and 8D). Since cellular metabolism is tightly related to macrophage functions15, we asked whether regulation of mitochondrial metabolism affected CD73 activity in CD19+ macrophages. Antimycin, an OXPHOS inhibitor, dramatically impaired CD73 activity (Supplementary Fig. 8D). Induction of reactive oxide species by diamide, rather than their removal by N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC), also inhibited CD73 activity. By contrast, blocking CD19 with neutralizing antibodies or inhibiting glycolysis with 2-deoxy-d-glucose (2-DG) had no effect on the CD73 activity (Supplementary Fig. 8D). Therefore, mitochondrial metabolism, but not CD19-associated cell signaling regulate the functions of CD19+ macrophages in the tumor. Consistent with the cell studies, conditional knocked out of Pax5 in mouse macrophages (Pax5flox/flox;Lyz-Cre, named as Pax5△Mφ) drastically inhibited the growth of orthotopically injected Hepa1-6-derived tumors (Fig.5L and Supplementary Fig. 8E-8G). As expected, depletion of PAX5 efficiently decreased the protein levels of CD19, CD73, and PD-L1 in the macrophages of these mice (Supplementary Fig. 8H). Collectively, these results suggested that PAX5, instead of CD19, plays a central role in the regulation of CD19+ macrophages in the tumor.

PAX5 induces PD-L1 and CD73 in a post-transcriptional manner
Interestingly, PAX5 overexpression in human THP1 cells did not significantly induce the mRNA levels of PD-L1 and CD73 (Fig. 6A), indicating post-transcriptional regulation of PAX5 in CD19+macrophages. We performed CUT&Tag (Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation) and RNA-seq assays on human THP-1 cells with or without PAX5 overexpression and identified global expression changes of genes that are transcriptionally regulated by PAX5 (Fig. 6B). Among these changes, genes associated with lysosome pathways were the second most significantly enriched, behind the genes involved in phagocytosis (Fig. 6C), suggesting that PAX5 may control target protein degradation via lysosome. Heat shock cognate 71-kDa protein (HSC70) is a chaperon protein that brings target proteins to lysosomes for degradation in cells29. We first performed mIHC on human HCC samples, specifically quantifying the protein co-expression patterns of PAX5, HSC70, CD19, PD-L1, and CD73 within CD19⁺TAMs. Results revealed that in CD19⁺TAMs, PAX5 expression exhibited significant positive correlations with the expression of CD19, PD-L1, and CD73. However, no correlation was observed between PAX5 and HSC70 protein levels in these cells (Supplementary Fig. 9A). These findings suggested that PAX5 is proposed to influence HSC70-mediated protein degradation by altering these interaction dynamics rather than changes in the total abundance of HSC70. We then identified three KFERQ-like motifs (CMA), which are potential binding sites to HSC70, in both PD-L1 and CD73 (Fig. 6D). Coimmunoprecipitation assays validated protein interactions between HSC70 and PD-L1 or CD73 (Fig. 6E), While KFERQ-like motif mutations in PD-L1 and CD73 disrupted their interactions with HSC70 compared to the wild type (WT) proteins (Supplementary Fig. 9B and 9C). In lysosome function assays, we observed that lysosomes were significantly inhibited upon PAX5 overexpression (Fig. 6F and Supplementary 6G). Meanwhile, both CD73 and PD-L1 were induced when PAX5-overexpresing THP-1 cells were treated with inhibitors of lysosomal proteolysis (NH4Cl and leupeptin) (Fig. 6H).

Because decreased number of lysosomes were seen in the PAX5-overexpressing THP-1 cells, we speculated that PAX5 may also regulate the activity of TFEB (Transcription Factor EB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis (Supplementary Fig. 10A)30, in the nucleus. We found that nuclear TFEB levels were dramatically diminished in PAX5-overexpressing cells (Fig. 6I and Supplementary Fig. 10B). Knockdown of TFEB inhibited lysosomal functions and increased PD-L1 and CD73 protein levels, similar to the effects of PAX5 overexpression (Supplementary Fig.10C-10E). Overexpression of TFEB offset the effects of PAX5 overexpression, leading to reduced levels of PD-L1 and CD73 in the PAX5-overexpressing cells (Supplementary Fig. 10F and 10G). We sought to delineate the mechanism by which PAX5 regulates the nuclear translocation of TFEB. TFEB subcellular translocation is regulated primarily by Ca2+ signaling or mTOR-mediated phosphorylation31,32. While no change in mTOR expression was observed in the PAX5-overexpressing cells (data not shown), we reasoned that increasing calcium uptake by mitochondria, due to their up-regulated biogenesis in CD19+ TAMs, may impact Ca2+ signaling in the cytosol32. Using a fluorescent probe, we found an increased level of mitochondrial Ca2+ and, accordingly, a decreased level of cytosolic Ca2+ in PAX5-overexpressing THP-1 cells (Fig. 6J). Treatment with IACS-010759 (an OXPHOS inhibitor) or ionomycin (a Ca2+ ionophore) significantly increased the cytosolic level of Ca2+ and thus promoted the nuclear level of TFEB (Supplementary Fig. 10H and 10I). These results suggested that PAX5 modulates the Ca2+ shuttling between mitochondria and the cytosol, consequently inhibiting the nuclear translocation of TFEB and lysosomal activity, which eventually increases the levels of CD73 and PD-L1 by inhibiting their lysosomal degradation.

Blocking CD19+ TAMs enhances the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade therapy
Given the role of CD19+ TAMs in HCC progression, we wanted to determine whether they could be a therapeutic target in treating HCC. In a syngeneic HCC tumor model, we first depleted macrophages in mice using clodronate liposomes every other day for four doses (Supplementary Fig. 11A-11C) prior to mouse Hepa1-6-derived tumor models establishment (Supplementary Fig. 11D)33,34. Control or Pax5-overexpressing iBMDMs were then infused into these mice to test their effects on tumor growth (Supplementary Fig. 11D). As expected, Pax5-overexpressing iBMDMs promoted greater tumor growth than wild-type iBMDMs (Supplementary Fig. 11E). In another orthotopic mouse model without systemic depletion of macrophages, Pax5-overexpressing iBMDMs also imposed a profound pro-tumor effect (Fig. 7A). Immunohistochemical analysis revealed that Pax5-overexpressing iBMDMs limited the tumor infiltration of CD8+ T cells (Fig. 7B), indicating an immunosuppressive TME.

CD19+ TAMs create an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment with increased levels of PD-L1 and CD73. We next tested whether the combination of PD-L1 and CD73 blockade had a synergistic effect on tumor control (Fig. 7C). Anti-CD73 neutralizing antibodies or a small-molecule inhibitor of CD73 significantly enhanced the anti-tumor effect of anti-PD-L1 antibodies in an orthotopic HCC mouse model (Fig. 7D). These effects are solely dependent on PAX5 in the CD19+ macrophages, as PD-L1 and CD73 blockade did not affect tumor progression in the Pax5△Mφ mice (Supplementary Fig. 11F). In the presence of anti-PD-L1 antibodies, CD73 blockade significantly increased the tumor infiltration of CD8+ T cells, as well as CD4+ T cells and natural killer cells. Tumor cell proliferation was greatly suppressed, as indicated by reduced Ki-67 staining (Supplementary Fig. 12).

Because induced mitochondrial respiration is critical for the functions of CD19+ TAMs, we tested whether inhibiting mitochondrial respiration of CD19+ TAMs had a similar anti-tumor effect. The OXPHOS inhibitor IACS-010759 exhibited an improved anti-tumor effect when combined with anti-PD-L1 antibodies in the orthotopic mouse HCC tumor model (Fig. 7E). The combination of PD-L1 blockade and OXPHOS inhibition also significantly promoted tumor infiltration of immune cells, including CD4+ T cells and CD8+ T cells (Supplementary Fig. 13). Collectively, therapeutic approaches targeting CD73 or OXPHOS -when optimized to leverage the heightened dependency of CD19+ TAMs on these pathways show great promise for improving the anti-tumor efficacy of immunotherapy for HCC.

## Methods

Ethics Statement
All animal experiments were approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital, School of Medicine, Zhejiang University (approval number:No. 2020-483). The maximal permitted tumor size/burden as stipulated by this ethics committee is a single tumor diameter of no more than 20 mm, or a total tumor volume per animal of no more than 2000 mm3; or tumor weight not exceeding 10% of the animal's body weight. All animals included in the study maintained tumor sizes/burden within the permitted limits, and no instances of exceeding the maximal tumor size/burden were recorded.

The collection and application of clinical samples were approved by the ethics committee of the First Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine (approval number:No. 2020-681). All patients’ informed consent was obtained.

A detailed description of the methods used in the study can be found in the Supplementary information.

Cell culture
THP-1 cells, Hepa1-6, Plat-E and HEK-293T cells were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA), immortalized murine bone marrow-derived macrophages (iBMDMs) were provided by Jingying Zhang at Zhejiang University. THP-1 cells were cultured in Roswell Park Memorial Institute medium (RPMI 1640, Gibco, Carlsbad, CA). Hepa1-6, Plat-E and HEK-293T cells were cultured in high-glucose Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM, Gibco). Media were supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Sigma-Aldrich, Saint Louis, MO), and maintained at 37.0 ± 0.2 °C in a humidified incubator with 5.0% CO2. BMDMs were isolated from femurs and tibia of adult C57BL/6 mice (The Model Animal Research Center of Nanjing University, Nanjing, China) and cultured in RPMI 1640 medium containing 50 ng/ml recombinant murine macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF, Peprotech, Rocky Hill, NJ) for 5-day differentiation.

Mouse models
All mice were bred under pathogen-free conditions. Animal experiments were approved by the ethics committee of The First Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine. The maximal permitted tumour size/burden for the study was defined as a longest diameter of 20 mm or a tumour burden equivalent to 10% of the animal’s body weight, in accordance with the ethical approval. Throughout the experimental period, none of the animals exceeded these predefined maximal tumour size or burden thresholds. Lyz-Cre mice were obtained from The Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME). Homozygous muMT mice were provided by Prof. Chao Wang at Zhejiang University. Pax5flox/flox and CD19flox/flox mice were purchased from Cyagen Biosciences (Suzhou, China). C57BL/6 (CD45.2) mice were purchased from The Model Animal Research Center of Nanjing University (Nanjing, China). Mice at 6-12 weeks of age were used for animal experiments.

For in situ mice model, a 20 μl suspension consisting of 50% Matrigel Basement Membrane Matrix (Corning, Teterboro, NJ) and 50% phosphate buffered saline (PBS; Cienry, Hangzhou, China) with Hepa1-6 cells in combination with macrophages were injected into the liver of mice. For syngeneic model, Hepa1-6 cells with 100 μl PBS were inoculated subcutaneously into the left or right flanks of mice. Sacrificed tumors were processed for further experiments.

Transfection of lentiviral vectors, siRNA and plasmid
THP-1 cells and iBMDMs were seeded in 6-well plates at a density of 2 × 105 cells/ml and infected with lenti-PAX5, lenti-TFEB or lenti-NC (Jikai, Shanghai, China). Stably transduced cells were purified using fluorescence activated cell sorting for further experiments. For siRNA transfection, 1.5 × 105 per well THP-1 cells were seeded in 24-well plates and transfected with human TFEB siRNA (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Santa Cruz, CA) using lipofectamine RNAimax (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) for 48 hours according to manufacturer’s protocols. For plasmids transfection, HEK-293T cells were seeded in suitable density, the plasmids were transfected with Lipo8000TM Transfection Reagent (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. After incubation for 24 h, the transfected cells were subjected to indicated analysis.

Targeted anti-CD19 CAR-T cell therapy
CD19+/CD19- macrophages were isolated from the spleens of mice (CD45+CD11b+F4/80+CD19+), and were mixed with Hepa1-6 cells to establish subcutaneous xenograft model at the left (CD19+ macrophages) or right (CD19- macrophages) flank of C57BL/6 or muMT mice. Anti-CD19 CAR-T cells were prepared and expanded. Mice were randomly assigned into groups for T cell infusion (1 × 107 cells in 100 µL PBS), and were sacrificed after 14 days. Harvested tumors were processed for subsequent experiments.

ImageStream analysis
Single-cell suspensions were stained and observed using an ImageStream II system (Amnis Corp, Seattle, WA) to identify CD19+ macrophages, CD19- macrophages, and B cells. Totally 1 × 105 single and focus cells were collected and analyzed by IDEASTM 6.2 software (Amnis Corp).

Multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC)
HCC and para-tumor were prepared into slides with 4-μm thickness. mIHC was performed using Opal™ 6-Plex Detection Kits (Akoya Biosciences, Marlborough, MA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and RNA-seq
ScRNA-seq libraries were constructed using a Chromium Single Cell 3’ Library and Gel Bead Kit v3.1 (10 x Genomics) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA-seq was performed using the Illumina Hiseq XTEN platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) at Novogene Co. Ltd (Beijing, China).

Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis was conducted using GraphPad Prism 8 (GraphPad Inc., La Jolla, CA).

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

the translational challenge of B cell toxicity in clinical settings. To address this, we are
implementing the following complementary strategies:
A. Dual-signal CAR-T design: Engineering CAR-T cells to require a second signal (e.g.,
tumor-specific cytokines or checkpoint molecules) that is only present in the TME.
B. AND-gate CARs: Developing dual-targeting CARs (e.g., CD19 + TAM-specific markers
such as CD163 or MARCO) to reduce off-target B cell depletion.
C. Hypoxia-activated CARs: Exploiting the low-oxygen tumor microenvironment to trigger
CAR-T activity selectively.
D. Intratumoral injection: Directly administering CAR-T cells into tumors (e.g., via
ultrasound or CT-guided intratumoral injection) to enhance local targeting and minimize
systemic exposure.
We are committed to translating these approaches to the clinic and providing a
precision treatment regimen for HCC patients. Thank you again for highlighting this critical
consideration, which has guided our focus on refining CAR-T specificity for clinical
applicability. Please let us know if further details on any of these strategies would
strengthen this aspect of our work.

Comment 6. PAX5 is a pro-B-cell factor and the above-mentioned previous study
(DOI: 10.1038/s41467-022-33117-y) has reported that the deficiency of PAX5 could
drive the macrophage differentiation. The authors should at least discuss how the
current study can be related to that finding. Because here the current study found
a positive role of PAX5 on the PD-L1 expression and tumor immunosuppression in
the TAM. It looks like the findings from these two studies are counteracting.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful perspective regarding the relationship
between our identified CD19+ TAMs and previously reported pro-B-cell-derived
macrophages (B-MFs). This comparison provides a valuable framework to contextualize
our findings, and we thank the opportunity to clarify key distinctions and connections:
While prior work has elegantly demonstrated that cancers can induce trans-differentiation
of bone marrow-derived B-cell precursors—specifically Csf1R⁺ Pax5Low pre-B cells and
immature IgM⁺ B cells—into TAMs (termed B-MFs) via M-CSF signaling. A defining
feature of B-MFs is the downregulation of PAX5 alongside upregulation of macrophage-
associated genes (CD68, Csf1r, Cebpb, Cebpg, Ccl2, Csf1), coupled with enhanced
phagocytic and immunosuppressive functions. Notably, these B-MFs are nearly absent
in μMT mice (which lack mature B cells), consistent with their origin from B-cell
lineage precursors.
In our study, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis revealed that CD19+
TAMs exhibit co-expression of B-cell (IGHM, IGHG) and macrophage (CD68, CSF1R)
gene modules (Fig 3C). Furthermore, in vivo studies demonstrate that CD19⁺ TAMs exist
at low frequencies under physiological conditions (see Figure S1D), including in μMT mice
(Figure S3H), and are enriched during tumor progression, where they promote
immunosuppression.
A key mechanistic distinction lies in the role of PAX5. In B-MFs, PAX5 is downregulated
as part of the trans-differentiation process from B-cell precursors to macrophages. In our
study, however, PAX5 functions not as a lineage repressor but as a transcriptional
activator within CD19⁺ TAMs: PAX5 overexpression in macrophages (THP-1 cells)
induces CD19 expression without suppressing macrophage markers (e.g., CD68, CSF1R).
Far from being contradictory, our findings and the prior report on B-MFs collectively
highlight the context-dependent functionality of PAX5 in regulating hematopoietic cell fate
and plasticity. While PAX5 loss drives myeloid commitment in progenitors, its
overexpression in mature macrophages promotes an immunosuppressive, mitochondrial-
rich TAM phenotype. We had expanded the Discussion section (Page 18, Line 11) to
explicitly address this context-dependent functionality and its implications for TAM biology.
Furthermore, our preliminary tracing studies suggest that CD19⁺ macrophages in
tumors originate from two sources: peripheral blood monocytes and tissue-resident
macrophages (For reviewer-Figure 9). However, the relative contribution of each
population remains to be quantified. We will perform more in vivo and in vitro models to
clarify the origination and cell differentiation of CD19+ macrophages in the future.

In this study, the authors compellingly identified CD19⁺ TAMs as a novel,
immunosuppressive subpopulation enriched in HCC and linked to poor prognosis. The

along with the specific revisions we have implemented (or plan to implement) in the revised

Major：
Comment 1. The authors should explicitly compare CD19⁺ TAMs with traditional
M1/M2-like features on their metabolic, transcriptional, and functional identities. Is

Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s interest in clarifying the relationship between
CD19⁺/CD19⁻ TAMs and classical M1/M2 polarization states. To address this, we
systematically compared these subsets as detailed.
To compare the classification of CD19⁺/CD19⁻ macrophages with M1/M2 polarization
states, we re-analyzed scRNA-seq data to profile their M1/M2 subtype markers,
inflammatory, metabolic, proliferative, and immune functional signatures. While CD19⁺
macrophages exhibited transcriptional proximity to M2-like macrophages, no strong
correlative associations were observed (Supplementary Table 8; see also Figure 3D).
CyTOF analysis further confirmed the presence of a classical M2-like subpopulation
(CD163⁺) within HCC tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), which is not entirely
identical to CD19⁺ TAMs (For reviewer-Figure 10).

human HCC tissues, including CD19+ TAMs, CD19- TAMs, and B cells (left) and CD19

In addition, flow cytometry validation of canonical M1/M2 markers revealed that
CD19⁺ TAMs expressed higher levels of M2-related markers than CD19⁻ TAMs (For
reviewer-Figure 11). However, no definite associations were found between the CD19+/
CD19- TAMs and M1/M2 classifications.

These data indicated that the CD19⁺/CD19⁻ axis represents a distinct dimension of
macrophage heterogeneity orthogonal to traditional M1/M2 polarization. Their unique co-
expression of B cell lineage markers, PAX5 dependency, and mitochondrial hyperactivity
further distinguish them as a functionally discrete TAM subset. We are conducting
additional in vivo and in vitro investigations to systematically characterize their
developmental provenance and lineage commitment processes, and clarify the positioning
of CD19⁺ macrophages within the established M1/M2 polarization spectrum.
Comment 2. Could CD19+ macrophages be fused cells between macrophage and B
cells, or macrophage with B cell endocytosed?
Response: We fully acknowledge the critical nature of your concerns and have addressed
the potential fusion or endocytosis hypotheses through a combination of single-cell
imaging, flow cytometry, and genetic modeling. These experiments now provide
conclusive evidence that CD19+ TAMs arise from transcriptional reprogramming rather
than cell fusion.
1) Fluorescence Distribution and Marker Analysis
Single-cell imaging flow cytometry staining and mIHC: High-resolution imaging revealed
non-uniform co-distribution of CD14 (macrophage marker) and CD19 within CD19⁺ TAMs.
Notably, CD19 fluorescence was not encapsulated by CD14 structures, ruling out
endocytosis of intact B cells, which would likely show membrane-bound CD19 signals (Fig
1C). Furthermore, CD19⁺ macrophages were uniformly negative for CD20, another B cell-
specific markers (Fig 1E).
2) Cell Size and Phenotypic Validation
Flow Cytometry Gating: Back-gating analysis of CD19⁺ macrophages exhibit a distinct
FSC/SSC values distribution from B cells (Fig S1C).
3) Genetic Model Validation
In B cell-deficient uMT mouse models, CD19⁺ TAMs were still detected, demonstrating
their development is independent of B cell presence (Fig S3H). This eliminates the
possibility that CD19⁺ expression arises from B cell fusion or phagocytosis, as both
processes would require intact B cells in the microenvironment. In WT mice, CD19⁺ TAMs
frequencies showed no correlation with B cell counts across tumor models (Fig. S1F),
further excluding B cell dependence.
Together, these results indicated that CD19⁺ macrophages were not derived from
macrophage-B cell fusion or B cell endocytosis. Their CD19 expression likely reflects a
unique transcriptional program, as supported by their distinct metabolic, transcriptional,
and functional profiles. Instead, CD19 expression arises from PAX5-driven transcriptional
reprogramming in myeloid cells.
Comment 3. Although the OXPHOS inhibitor IACS-010759 exhibited an improved
anti-tumor effect, the authors could not attribute the function to CD19 macrophages,
since tumor cells or other cells can also be targeted by this inhibitor.
Response： We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's insightful comment concerning the
potential outside-target effects of IACS-010759. As a pharmacological OXPHOS inhibitor,
IACS-010759 may indeed exert effects not only on CD19+ TAMs but also on other cell
types within the tumor microenvironment (TME), including tumor cells and stromal
populations.
However, previous studies have indicated that M2-TAMs exhibit high OXPHOS activity
and are characterized by an enhanced spare respiratory capacity, which supports their
immunosuppressive function (PMID: 33407885, 26649578). In contrast, tumor cells in
hypoxic regions, particularly in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), primarily rely on
glycolysis for energy metabolism (PMID: 29171040, 33398194). More importantly, our
data demonstrate that OXPHOS inhibition combined with anti-PD-L1 treatment
significantly remodels the immune microenvironment (Supplementary figure S12),
specifically by reducing CD19+ TAMs (For reviewer-Figure 12) and enhancing antitumor
immunity. These findings suggest that targeting CD19+ TAMs is a major contributor to the
observed antitumor response.

While we cannot definitively ascribe the entire therapeutic effect exclusively to CD19+

efficacy of immunotherapy for HCC.” in the manuscript to ensure more precise
descriptions of this relationship. Additionally, we plan to conduct further experiments to
dissect the cell type-specific effects of IACS-010759 in future studies, which will help
clarify the contributions of different cell populations to the therapeutic outcome.
Comment 4. The last sentence “Collectively, therapeutic approaches targeting
CD73 or OXPHOS in CD19 + TAMs show great promise for improving the anti-tumor
efficacy of immunotherapy for HCC.” is not acceptable. The authors need to discuss
more about how their findings could translate to therapeutical approaches.
OXPHOS and CD73 are all non-specific to CD19 macrophages and might not be
good targets for developing new therapies.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s critical and insightful comments, which
highlight a key consideration for translating our findings into therapeutic strategies. We
fully agree that OXPHOS and CD73 are not exclusive to CD19⁺ TAMs, and their non-
specificity poses challenges for the development of targeted therapies.
While OXPHOS and CD73 are not unique to CD19⁺ TAMs, our data reveal that CD19⁺
TAMs in HCC exhibit a selectively heightened dependency on these pathways to exert
their immunosuppressive functions. Specifically, CD19⁺ TAMs display significantly higher
OXPHOS activity and CD73 expression compared to CD19⁻ TAMs, whereas HCC tumor
cells primarily rely on glycolysis—consistent with their hypoxic microenvironment. Notably,
CD19⁺ TAMs and HCC cells show comparable levels of CD73 and PD-L1 expression (For
reviewer-Figure 13), our functional data highlight a distinct role of CD19⁺ TAMs in
mediating the effects of these pathways: in vivo studies using Pax5△MΦ mice (which
specifically deplete CD19⁺ TAMs) demonstrated that blockade of PD-L1 and CD73 no
longer impacted tumor progression (Figure S10F). This suggests that CD19⁺ TAMs are
critical mediators of the immunosuppressive effects exerted by these molecules.
